item.title: AI chatbots are becoming political advisers. Their answers can mislead voters
item.description:
AI chatbots are becoming political advisers. Their answers can mislead voters
November 2, 20263:02 PM ET
By
Katie McQue
About half of American adults reported using AI-powered chatbots and about 42% of users said they use them to search for information, according to a Pew Research Center survey from earlier this year.
Jon Cherry/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Jon Cherry/Getty Images
Voters are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for information ahead of the midterms, yet many of the most popular ones may give misleading information about candidates and polling site opening times, according to researchers. Some chatbots have even provided lists of candidates to vote for, raising concerns among experts that AI-generated misinformation could influence voters' decisions.

item.title: Judge accuses DOJ of 'weaponization,' tosses case against ex-FBI officials
item.description:

Judge accuses DOJ of 'weaponization,' tosses case against ex-FBI officials
Updated November 2, 20262:31 PM ET
Originally published November 2, 20261:54 PM ET
Ryan Lucas
Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui speaks before a debate at the Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, D.C. in November 2024.
Craig Hudson/The Washington Post via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Craig Hudson/The Washington Post via Getty Images
A federal magistrate judge on Monday dismissed the Justice Department's criminal case against two former FBI officials charged in connection with the bureau's investigations into former President Joe Biden's son.
Bradley Benavides and Nikki Floris were charged around two weeks ago with lying to Congress in 2023 about their knowledge of the FBI's investigations into Biden's son, Hunter Biden. It is one of several politically charged actions by the Justice Department under President Trump in the run-up to the midterm elections on Tuesday.
At a hearing in federal court in Washington, D.C., U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui castigated the government's investigation into Floris and Benavides, describing it as rushed and riddled with errors.

item.title: DOJ asks for Supreme Court to intervene on California ballot demands
item.description:
Elections
DOJ asks for Supreme Court to intervene on California ballot demands
Updated November 2, 202612:47 PM ET
Originally published November 2, 202611:34 AM ET
By
Jude Joffe-Block
The U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 14.
Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
A day before Election Day, the Department of Justice is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to wade into its unprecedented feud with California over the state's voter rolls.
The appeal is the department's latest foray into state election administration, which a federal judge referred to last week as "a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials."
After that judge, David Carter, a Clinton appointee, and a divided 9th Circuit Court of Appeals panel rejected the DOJ's request to order California to set aside and stop processing the ballots of thousands of people, the DOJ filed a notice Monday that it is seeking injunctive relief from the high court.
It remains to be seen whether the Supreme Court will agree to intervene and, if so, whether it would weigh in before Tuesday's Election Day.

item.title: When it comes to election pressure, this year's Georgia or Michigan could be anywhere
item.description:
Voting
When it comes to election pressure, this year's Georgia or Michigan could be anywhere
November 2, 20265:00 AM ET
Miles Parks
A sign directs residents to a polling place in Dearborn, Mich., on Aug. 4.
Scott Olson/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Scott Olson/Getty Images
There's one big difference, Tina Barton says, between running an election in a battleground state and a non-battleground.
It's what happens when there are mistakes.
"If a human error happens, it's easily explained in the press and it's not a story," Barton says. "You have a human error in a battleground state and all of a sudden it can become a massive conspiracy."
Barton would know.
In 2020, she oversaw elections as city clerk of Rochester Hills, Mich. On election night, her office mistakenly sent an unofficial absentee vote file twice because the first one didn't initially appear to send.
Elections

Such mistakes happen every election cycle in a national process run by tens of thousands of human beings. A machine isn't plugged in. A poll worker sleeps through their alarm clock ...

item.title: 6 things to watch for on election night
item.description:
6 things to watch for on election night
November 2, 20265:00 AM ET
Domenico Montanaro
People walk by a sign for voting on November 1, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. Michigan has become a focal point in the upcoming midterm elections, with a close race between Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI), and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that could decide who controls the chamber.
Spencer Platt/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Spencer Platt/Getty Images
It can be hard to know what to focus on in midterm elections. There are so many races, from elections for governor and senator to the House and state legislatures. For a better idea of how the night might go to see which party might control Congress, here are six things to watch:
1. The early bellwethers for Republican turnout and the Latino vote
There are two states, Indiana and Kentucky, that will see results in the 6 p.m. ET hour. And then there's Florida, which is split between the Eastern and Central time zones. But most of the state is on Eastern time. So lots of House race results will be coming in during the 7 p.m. ET hour, even if statewide contests like the Senate and governors races won't be called at the earliest until 8 p.m. ET.
